title: Q&A: Allison Jornlin Talks Milwaukee Ghosts in Her New Book
excerpt: Allison Jornlin’s American Ghost Walks tour service inspired her new book “In The Shadow of City Hall,” that dissects Milwaukee ghost hauntings in the city’s most iconic locations.
content:
Milwaukee’s history of the paranormal stretches beyond the walls of The Pfister Hotel, to the Miller Inn, Milwaukee Public Museum and all along Wisconsin Avenue. Our city’s rich history isn’t all suds and sunshine with our oldest buildings haunted by tragedy, mishap and scores still unsettled.

Allison Jornlin, a former elementary school teacher and current explorer (and tour guide) of all things haunted Milwaukee has compiled a richly informative book about Cream City’s paranormal past and present called “In The Shadow of City Hall.” The book will premiere at Milwaukee Paracon, this Saturday Oct. 17 from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. at Kochanski’s, with Jornlin speaking at 11:30 a.m. The conference is free to attend and her book will be available for online purchase Oct. 18.

I spoke with Allison Jornlin about her origins in haunted exploration, the impact of the film “Ghostbusters (1984)” and the history of the paranormal in Milwaukee.

Celebrate this year’s winners of the Betty Awards!

Did you always have an interest in the paranormal growing up?

I talk about it in the first chapter of my new book, when we were kids by the radio, my brother Mike Huberty and I consider our late mom responsible. We grew up in Big Bend, Wisconsin but my mom loved to listen to WGN in Chicago. Every Halloween, they would have Richard Crowe on, as Chicagoland’s ghost hunter, and he was like, “you could be a ghost hunter, that could be your career.” And I remember being excited about it then. As a kid, listening to Richard Crowe spin these tales upon a Chicagoland, it really inspired me.

I’m always interested in the edge of the known, those eternal questions of what happens when we die and are we alone in the universe and all of that. I think that always intrigued me as a kid, but it’s always been more intriguing than scary.

Are there shows or films in recent years that have been inspiring to you, or you found you know really interesting on a paranormal level?

I loved “X Files” and “Buffy the Vampire Slayer.” I’m not interested in reality TV ghost hunting, I don’t feel there’s a lot of reality in that. As younger people, an interesting movie for us was “Ghostbusters.” Although it’s a comedy, Dan Aykroyd actually wrote a book with his dad about the history of ghosts, and his family in Canada was very much into exploring spiritualism. They had séance circles at their house regularly, and so Aykroyd wrote that film from a lot of knowledge of having Society for Psychical Research journals in the house and in doing a lot of reading. It’s all taken to a degree to make it hilarious, but it’s based in reality in a lot of ways.

Tell us a bit about your new book to get our October fright going.

So the idea was to write a book that covers all the stories from those tour routes with more details on additional sites that you can’t put on the tour. It covers all the stuff close to city hall and then also Wisconsin Avenue. There’s going to be a lot of new stuff, and it’s like the tip of an iceberg. That’s why I started with Uncle Charlie at the Pfister. So I could start with something that people know well, but then dig down to some aspects of it that maybe they haven’t thought about, and then progressively get more detailed and obscure about hauntings nearby. I go further back in history as well, way way back.

What do you think makes Milwaukee such a great area for paranormal investigation?

Well, like any old city, we’ve had tragedies. We’ve had dark parts of our history for sure there’s so much that hasn’t been talked about yet. I think when you scratch beneath the surface you see where all these stories that people have been keeping under wraps. Like when I found out about the Miller Caves at Miller Inn, they were very open to the fact that they’re haunted and have invited me in alongside paranormal investigators.

It was so interesting to hear about these haunts at major institutions and public places in Milwaukee that have these stories behind them, like the Milwaukee Public Museum. The chief ghost Dr. Stephan Francis de Borhegyi, was the director from 1959 to 1969. He was really a beloved figure, and his life was cut short in a car crash on September 26, 1969. People believe that he haunts the museum, lingering around the artifacts that he collected on the third floor and mezzanine. I’ll be at MPM in October in the Streets of Old Milwaukee for Halloween Hauntings.

Tell us more about your background before leading the tours.

I was an elementary school teacher for 13 years. In 2008 I launched this haunted history tour and you know, when you’re consistent that’s how you succeed. My brother lives in Madison. I convinced him to start doing history tours there in 2010 and then it was his idea to go national. I’m like, “Okay now we’re both professional weirdos.” We get to do this full time. I love it.

Tell us more about the American Ghost Walks

What I do for American Ghost Walks is preserving folklore and put it in the tours in a way that’s entertaining, but also teaches you something about the culture of the city. Nobody has to believe in ghost stories to enjoy tours. They just have to understand that people everywhere tell these stories based on history. I started with Milwaukee, my hometown, and now we’re in eight states including Puerto Rico, St. Thomas and the Virgin Islands. I’ve written tours for the Big Island in Hawaii, and for southeastern Alaska; it’s really fun to explore these things from that folkloric perspective, and what you can learn about people of that area, what they feared.

How does one of your paranormal investigations get going?

When I have someone approach me about needing an investigation, I pass that on to Noah Leigh, because he’s the expert (Paranormal Investigators of Milwaukee, also known as PIM, was founded by Leigh in 2007). I’ve been on a lot of paranormal investigations with them, but I don’t have the expertise in designing experiments like he does. He’s a working scientist with a lot of equipment and a lot of knowledge.

What’ll surprise people about the book?

People will be surprised by some of Wisconsin Avenue because there’s so many hauntings from end to end. We have a tour called the Shadow of City Hall that we’ve been doing for a while. And then we’ve recently added a Brady Street tour as well.
